title: Verifier‑Augmented vs. LLM‑Only NetOps Agents: A Paired Evaluation on an Action‑Aware Staging Benchmark
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark (ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1). The preregistered design (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) used gpt-5-mini as the generator, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer, N=400 paired tasks (800 episodes), and shared_initial_generation semantics (one shared LLM candidate per task delivered to both conditions). Confirmatory outcomes (archived artifacts) show complete_pairs = 400; baseline_success_rate = 1.0 (400/400); guarded_success_rate = 1.0 (400/400); paired contingency n_11 = 400, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0; observed paired difference = 0.0; preregistered permutation p = 1.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples); Cohen's h = 0.0. We explicitly and prominently report that two preregistered design choices—shared_initial_generation semantics and reuse of the same deterministic validator as both runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer—produced a deterministic ceiling effect (universal acceptance) that rendered the primary estimand uninformative for assessing generator×guard closed‑loop dynamics in this run. We present the artifact‑grounded execution and analysis, diagnose why the design produced a null outcome, report representative task difficulty diagnostics, and provide artifact‑grounded recommendations to harden future benchmarks so they expose generator×guard interactions.

sections.introduction:
Generative LLMs are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent into network configuration artifacts and staged operational actions (canaries, progressive rollouts, rollback). Prior work demonstrates that LLMs can synthesize syntactically plausible configurations but cautions that operational safety depends on end‑to‑end behaviors that include generation variance, deterministic verification, staged rollout semantics, repair, rollback, and provenance. To probe whether adding a deterministic runtime verifier meaningfully changes end‑to‑end safety outcomes, we preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) on ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1.

Research question. Under ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1, does integrating a deterministic runtime validator with an LLM generator increase the paired safe‑deploy rate relative to an LLM‑only pipeline? The primary estimand was the paired difference in safe‑deploy rate (guarded − baseline) under a paired binary design with N=400 tasks.

Key contribution and central outcome. We provide a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5, and we archive execution and analysis artifacts for reproducibility. The run produced a deterministic ceiling: identical shared generator outputs were delivered to both conditions and the deterministic validator accepted every shared candidate, producing identical safe‑deploy outcomes (100% safe‑deploy in both conditions). This ceiling makes the primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard interaction in this run. We (a) present the exact, artifact‑grounded confirmatory statistics, (b) diagnose the design and implementation factors that produced the ceiling, and (c) provide concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations to avoid this failure mode in future preregistered evaluations.
sections.related_work:
Intent→configuration pipelines, IaC automation, and verifier‑guided generate–validate–repair architectures contextualize this study. Recent intent‑to‑configuration demonstrations (intent‑based translation, PreConfig, GraphSynth) show LLMs can generate usable network or IaC templates in benchmark settings, but evaluations are typically on curated corpora or testbeds. In IaC contexts, verifier‑guided loops (e.g., TerraFormer) report correctness gains that motivate similar integrations for NetOps; however, closed‑loop runtime verifier utility under staged rollout semantics remains underexplored.

Deterministic verifiers and reachability tools (header‑space and related verifiers) are effective at finding configuration errors offline but vary in modeling assumptions and scope (Kubernetes vs. IP networks, overlay vs. underlay). Agentic and tool‑augmented LLM architectures (ReAct, RAG, multi‑agent orchestrations) extend functionality for AIOps and root‑cause analysis but introduce failure modes—hallucination, misapplied tools, and miscalibrated confidence—that motivate runtime guardrails and staged deployment. Multiple surveys and recent system papers highlight an evaluation gap: action‑aware benchmarks that combine generation, runtime blocking, staged rollouts, repair, rollback, and provenance are not yet standardized. This study operationalizes a compact action‑aware staging benchmark under a strict preregistered design to probe verifier utility under those constraints.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory estimand. The experiment was preregistered as cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1. The confirmatory design fixed N=400 paired tasks, a paired binary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, and a permutation‑based paired test (two‑sided, α=0.05). An exact McNemar two‑sided test was prespecified as corroboration. Bootstrap percentile CIs (seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) were frozen for secondary summaries.

Adapter semantics and shared generation (critical design choice). Execution used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family with requested generator gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer. Crucially, preregistration set shared_initial_generation = true (independent_condition_generation = false): a single deterministic LLM generation was performed per task and that identical candidate was delivered to both the baseline and guarded episodes. This choice was made to isolate the validator’s acceptance behavior on identical outputs (it intentionally removed independent generator variance across conditions). Model_call accounting therefore differs from episode counts: planned episodes = 800 (two episodes per task) while model_calls_used = 400 (one shared LLM call per task). The execution manifest confirms these values.

Episode flow, validator policy, repair budget, and deterministic replay. For each task the adapter: (1) requested a shared initial candidate from gpt‑5‑mini; (2) delivered it to baseline and guarded episodes; (3) in the guarded episode deterministic_netops_validator_v5 applied full intent‑constraint validation and, per the preregistered repair policy, could invoke up to one repair attempt. The validator recorded validator_trace entries containing repair_applied flags, normalized_configuration, validation_before/after states, difficulty metadata, and final validity. In this run repair_applied = false for all episodes. The preregistration mandated deterministic three‑replay consistency checks (replay each agent+simulator pair three times); tasks failing replay consistency or hitting simulator errors were to be flagged and excluded from the primary analysis. All deterministic consistency checks passed; no exclusions were applied.

Task generation and difficulty labeling. Tasks were generated deterministically with deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Each task included structured difficulty metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, pattern, required_command_count, and level ∈ {medium, hard, very_hard}). Representative manifest entries (first six tasks) record level counts: medium = 1, hard = 2, very_hard = 3; the full per‑task labels for N=400 are archived in the task manifest for auditor aggregation. Inclusion/exclusion rules, missingness handling, and contamination checks were automated and performed without human adjudication as preregistered.

sections.discussion:
Why the primary estimand became uninformative. Two preregistered design decisions combined to create the deterministic ceiling. First, shared_initial_generation delivered identical generator outputs to baseline and guarded episodes, intentionally removing between‑condition generator variance. Second, the runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer were the same deterministic implementation (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). When identical inputs are judged by the same deterministic validator, acceptance decisions necessarily concord and the paired difference collapses to zero. Thus the observed null result is a direct artifact of the frozen design and not evidence that runtime verification is universally unnecessary.

Consequences for statistical power and interpretability. The preregistered power calculation assumed a non‑ceiling baseline rate and intra‑pair variability such that a ≈10 percentage‑point absolute difference would be detectable with N=400. The realized ceiling invalidates those assumptions: permutation and McNemar tests correctly reflect identical outcomes (p = 1.0) but do not permit inference about generator×guard closed‑loop dynamics. Researchers should therefore ensure preregistered designs preserve non‑zero baseline error rates and generator variance when evaluating runtime guard interventions.

Artifact‑grounded recommendations to harden future action‑aware benchmarks. Based on archived traces and preregistration semantics we recommend: (1) independent_condition_generation = true so each arm receives an independently sampled generator output (restores generator variance); (2) separate runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer implementations or independent scorers to avoid self‑concordant adjudication; (3) controlled adversarial seeding (preregistered perturbation fraction) to guarantee measurable baseline failure rates; (4) difficulty‑stratified sampling or oversampling of very_hard patterns to ensure nontrivial error rates; (5) instrumented repair and rollback metrics (enable and log repair_applied, repair attempts, and rollback durations) as preregistered secondary outcomes. These steps are directly implementable because the validator_trace schema already records repair_applied, validation_before/after, difficulty metadata, and normalized_configuration.

Threats to validity and generalizability. Model and scope: a single declared generator (gpt‑5‑mini) and a single deterministic validator were used; results do not generalize across models, verifier families, or production heterogeneity. Construct validity: using the same deterministic implementation for runtime guarding and post‑hoc scoring conflates acceptance and scoring. Environment realism: the benchmark is synthetic and the simulator/validator do not model production telemetry noise or adversarial actors. Adversarial robustness and human‑in‑the‑loop efficacy were not exercised and remain open research directions.

Operational implications. For NetOps practitioners evaluating verifier integration, our artifact‑grounded diagnosis yields two practical lessons: (i) benchmark and semantics choices that remove generation variance can hide the actual effect of runtime guards; (ii) independent adjudication channels (distinct scorers or human reviewers) are important to measure guard impact reliably. Benchmarks intended to validate runtime safety mechanisms should be preregistered with generation and scorer independence and explicit adversarial or difficulty stratification.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark. Under the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator pairing, every shared candidate satisfied the deterministic runtime validator and both conditions produced 100% safe‑deploy across N=400 pairs (paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0). This deterministic ceiling effect resulted from preregistered design and implementation homogeneity and renders the primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard closed‑loop interactions in this run. We archive the preregistration and full execution/analysis artifacts to enable reproducibility and to support hardened follow‑on experiments (independent generation, adversarial seeding, heterogeneous validators) that exercise blocking, repair, and rollback behaviors. Our artifact‑grounded hardening recommendations provide concrete steps researchers can preregister to preserve statistical signal when evaluating runtime verifier utility in NetOps settings.

limitations: Benchmark hardness and ceiling effect: under preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 so the guard had no opportunity to alter outcomes; this makes the primary estimand effectively untestable in this run and invalidates the original power rationale.

Model and scope: the experiment used a single generator (gpt-5-mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); results do not generalize across models, validators, or production heterogeneity.

Construct validity: the same deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementation served as both runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer; this conflation produces concordant acceptance/scoring and limits inference about independent closed‑loop verifier utility.

Shared candidate semantics: preregistered shared_initial_generation (one LLM generation per task shared by both conditions) intentionally reduces generation variance and therefore limits inference to the validator’s behavior on identical candidates rather than full generator+guard closed‑loop interactions.

Synthetic environment and external validity: the simulator and validator do not fully model production telemetry noise, operator workflows, or adversarial actor behaviours; external validity to live networks is limited.

Adversarial robustness untested: adversarial or distribution‑shifted prompts and generator faults that could trigger guard interventions were not exercised in this run and remain open for future work.

Aggregated difficulty reporting: the full per‑task difficulty labels for all N=400 are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and auditors can aggregate them reproducibly; the manuscript reports representative sample counts from the manifest (first six tasks: medium = 1, hard = 2, very_hard = 3) rather than an aggregate computed internally here to avoid presenting a derived summary that is not itself an archived artifact in the manuscript bundle.
